interview_metadata.name: Pedro Jimenez
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) ??? Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born in Yakima, Washington, in 1950, the oldest boy in a Mexican family. My parents had come up from Jalisco in the 1950s for farm and packing work, and at home we spoke Spanish, ate what my mother cooked, and kept the old holidays like Posadas and Dia de los Muertos. School was all right for me but I was better with my hands than with books, so I left after tenth grade and went to work early. I did orchard work, small construction jobs, and later became the kind of handyman people called when a faucet leaked, a door frame sagged, or a porch step needed replacing. In my twenties I moved toward the Puyallup area because there was steadier work and I liked the quieter pace. I married my wife Rosa in the early 1970s, and we raised three children, all grown now. The big events in my life were building a life without much schooling, buying our small house, seeing my children do better than me, and learning after retirement that I still needed to be useful, so I started volunteering at the senior center.

follow_ups.question: What do you remember most clearly about your childhood home?
follow_ups.response: The kitchen. My mother would have beans going, tortillas wrapped in a towel, and music playing low on the radio. We did not have much, but there was always a lot of noise, cousins coming in and out, and my father sharpening tools or fixing something after work.

follow_ups.question: How did leaving school affect the rest of your life?
follow_ups.response: It made me work harder with my hands, and it also made me a little careful around paperwork. I can read and handle bills, but I always wished I had finished. That is why I pushed my own kids to stay in school.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yes, the big crossroads was when I was about 24 and deciding whether to stay around Yakima doing seasonal work or move west where there was more repair and construction work. My father wanted me close, because family was everything to him, but I had just married Rosa and I wanted a steadier life. We packed what we had into an old car and came toward Puyallup, staying first with a cousin in Tacoma. I took any job I could find, then slowly people learned I could repair things and not overcharge them. That move made me more independent. It also gave my children a different kind of childhood than mine, more settled and more Northwest than farm camp.

follow_ups.question: What made Puyallup feel like the right place to settle?
follow_ups.response: It was close enough to work but not too big. There were older houses that needed repairs, garden space, and people minded their business but were friendly once they knew you.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone help you during that move?
follow_ups.response: My cousin Manuel let us sleep in his spare room for a few weeks. Rosa also kept me calm because I was worried about money every day then.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a choice, but not a fancy one. I looked at the money coming in, looked at Rosa, and knew I could not raise a family on maybes.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk it through with Rosa before deciding?
follow_ups.response: Yes, at the kitchen table late at night. She was nervous too, but she said if I found steady work she would make the home part work.

follow_ups.question: How long did it take to feel like the choice was right?
follow_ups.response: Maybe two years. Once we had regular customers and our first child was comfortable in school, I stopped thinking we might have to go back.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Maybe someone could have helped with job placement or classes, but I did not know how to ask. Back then I mostly trusted family and my own two hands.

follow_ups.question: Would adult education have helped you then?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially English paperwork, licenses, and bookkeeping. I learned those things slowly and made mistakes.

follow_ups.question: Who did you rely on most instead?
follow_ups.response: Rosa, my cousin Manuel, and a few older men from church who would tell me which contractors paid on time.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am married to Rosa, and we have been married a little over fifty years. She is the main person in my life, the one who knows when I am pretending not to worry. We have three grown children: Elena, who lives in Tacoma and works in a medical office; Marco, who is in Federal Way and does warehouse supervision; and Luis, who lives closer to Puyallup and works with computers. We have six grandchildren, and they come by mostly on Sundays or birthdays, though the older ones are busy. Family meals are still important to me. If I make tamales or pozole, I make too much on purpose so somebody takes containers home.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your children and grandchildren?
follow_ups.response: Luis stops by maybe once a week, Elena about twice a month, and Marco when his schedule allows. The grandchildren are more scattered, but Sunday afternoon is still the best chance.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Rosa do together day to day?
follow_ups.response: We have breakfast together around 7:30, watch some evening news, and go to church most Sundays. She reminds me about pills, and I carry the heavier groceries.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: I have a younger sister, Teresa, in Yakima, and a brother, Raul, in California. We talk by phone, not every week, but enough to know what is happening.

follow_ups.question: Who are you closest to among your siblings?
follow_ups.response: Teresa. She remembers the same family stories, and we talk in Spanish when one of us is missing our parents.

follow_ups.question: Do they visit Puyallup?
follow_ups.response: Teresa comes maybe once a year. Raul does not travel much anymore, so mostly we call.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Outside family, I have friends from the senior center and the walking club. There is Frank, who used to be a mechanic, and Howard, who always thinks he knows the right way to prune roses. We play cards sometimes on Thursday afternoons, and I help a few older neighbors with small repairs if they cannot afford a contractor. These are not dramatic friendships, but they are steady. At my age steady is worth a lot.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually do with those friends?
follow_ups.response: Walk, drink coffee after the walk, play cards, and argue gently about baseball. Sometimes one of them brings a tool that needs fixing.

follow_ups.question: How often are you at the senior center?
follow_ups.response: Usually two or three times a week, more if I am giving a repair or gardening workshop.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We live in Puyallup, in a quiet neighborhood with older houses, small lawns, and people who wave but do not always stop to talk. There are families with kids, retired couples, and a few renters who change every couple years. I like that I can get to the grocery store, church, the senior center, and the trail without too much trouble. The traffic has gotten heavier over the years, especially toward South Hill, but our street still feels manageable. I have a vegetable garden in back with tomatoes, chilies, cilantro, and some herbs.

follow_ups.question: Who do you know best on your street?
follow_ups.response: Our neighbor Mrs. Callahan two doors down. I fixed her gate once, and now she brings us apples in the fall.

follow_ups.question: What places nearby are part of your regular routine?
follow_ups.response: The senior center, Fred Meyer or WinCo for groceries, church on Sunday, and the Elma-Puyallup trail when the weather is not too wet.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe. I lock the shed because tools can walk away, but I am not afraid to take a morning walk.

follow_ups.question: Has anything happened that made you more cautious?
follow_ups.response: A few years ago someone went through unlocked cars on the block. Since then I keep the porch light on and lock the garage.

follow_ups.question: Does Rosa feel safe there too?
follow_ups.response: Mostly, yes. She does not like being alone after dark if I am out, but that is rare now.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The good part is peace, garden space, and knowing where everything is. The hard part is rising costs, traffic, and seeing old neighbors move away.

follow_ups.question: What change bothers you most?
follow_ups.response: The cost of repairs and property taxes. Even small things feel expensive on a fixed income.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you from moving?
follow_ups.response: This house fits us, and my garden is here. Also, moving would cost money and energy I do not want to spend.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it is just me and Rosa in the house. We have our routines, and the place is set up for two older people. I handle yard work, small repairs, and some cooking. Rosa does laundry, keeps track of family birthdays, and does a lot of the church phone calls, though we both share chores more than we used to. Nobody else is staying here now.

follow_ups.question: Do your grandchildren ever sleep over?
follow_ups.response: The younger ones used to. Now it is mostly a holiday or if a parent needs help for one night.

follow_ups.question: How do you divide household tasks?
follow_ups.response: I cook two or three dinners a week and do outside chores. Rosa keeps the calendar and bills organized with me checking the numbers.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent. It is just Rosa and me.

follow_ups.question: No one staying short-term right now?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

follow_ups.question: Has that changed recently?
follow_ups.response: No, it has been just us for many years.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Sometimes a grandchild stays one night, but not regularly.

follow_ups.question: How often would you say that happens?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a few times a year.

follow_ups.question: Who is most likely to stay?
follow_ups.response: Our granddaughter Sofia if her parents have something early the next day.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No. Nobody else usually lives here.

follow_ups.question: No one away for school or medical care?
follow_ups.response: No, thank God.

follow_ups.question: Has anyone stayed with you after a medical issue before?
follow_ups.response: Only short visits after surgeries in the family, not as part of the household.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Most days I wake up around 6:30, check my blood pressure, make coffee, and go look at the garden before breakfast. Mondays and Wednesdays I often go walking with the senior walking club if the weather is decent. Tuesdays I may be at the senior center doing a repair workshop or helping set up tables. Thursdays are sometimes cards and coffee. Fridays are errands with Rosa, and weekends are family, church, Mariners baseball when it is season, or Seahawks in the fall.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually work in the garden?
follow_ups.response: Morning, around 8:30 to 10:00, before my knees get stiff and before the sun is too strong.

follow_ups.question: What does a slower day look like?
follow_ups.response: I read, sharpen tools, do a crossword, maybe make salsa, and take a short walk around the block.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I do not work for pay anymore. I am retired from handyman work, which was mostly home repair, carpentry, plumbing fixes, painting, and whatever people needed. Now I volunteer at the local senior center, usually in the late morning or early afternoon. I show people how to patch drywall, fix a loose hinge, sharpen pruners, or get a garden bed ready. I try to keep the workshops practical, and I admit I like when my demonstration comes out cleaner than Frank's.

follow_ups.question: How often do you teach those workshops?
follow_ups.response: Usually twice a month, sometimes more in spring when people want garden help.

follow_ups.question: Do you still take paid repair jobs?
follow_ups.response: No regular ones. I might help a neighbor, but I do not charge like a business anymore.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I keep the household budget notebook, or at least I keep my version of it. I write down utilities, groceries, medicine, and any repair costs. I also check the car once a month, oil, tires, fluids, because older cars need attention. I translate little things for older neighbors sometimes, like a notice from the city or a doctor's appointment reminder. At home I also make sure Rosa's heavier chores do not fall on her.

follow_ups.question: When do you usually sit down with the budget?
follow_ups.response: First week of the month after Social Security deposits. I use a notebook and a calculator.

follow_ups.question: What car maintenance do you still do yourself?
follow_ups.response: Oil checks, tire pressure, wiper blades, battery terminals, small things. I do not crawl under the car much anymore.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest change is I check my blood pressure more faithfully now. My doctor got after me last year because the numbers were creeping up. I also walk a little slower and stretch my knees before I go out. Rosa and I have been trying to eat less salt, though I still overdo it with pozole sometimes. I have cut back on driving at night, because my eyes do not like glare.

follow_ups.question: How often do you check your blood pressure?
follow_ups.response: Most mornings, before coffee if I remember. I write the numbers in a little pad.

follow_ups.question: What changed in your cooking because of that?
follow_ups.response: More lime, garlic, and roasted chilies for flavor, less salt. Rosa still catches me reaching for the shaker.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: My children are grown now, so I do not have school routines in my house. When they were young, Rosa got them ready early, and I was usually gone to work before they left. They did homework at the kitchen table, and there were school concerts, soccer for Marco, and church activities. Now I hear more about my grandchildren's schedules, which are busier than anything we had.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with grandchildren's school routines now?
follow_ups.response: Only once in a while, like a pickup if someone is stuck at work.

follow_ups.question: What activities do your grandchildren do?
follow_ups.response: One plays soccer, one does band, and the older ones mostly work part-time or study.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: For myself, mostly traffic stops and neighborhood things. I have been pulled over for a taillight and for rolling through a stop sign many years ago. The officers were businesslike, not friendly exactly, but nothing terrible happened. When I was younger and brown men were standing around after work, you could feel police looking at you differently. I learned to keep my hands visible and speak calmly.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever called police yourself?
follow_ups.response: Once when someone was going through cars on the block. They took a report, but I do not think anything came of it.

follow_ups.question: Do you trust police in your area?
follow_ups.response: Somewhat. I think some do good work, but I do not assume everyone gets treated the same.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: One time my son Marco was stopped as a teenager walking home with friends. They had done nothing, but police questioned them like they were trouble.

follow_ups.question: How did that affect your son?
follow_ups.response: He was angry and embarrassed. I told him to stay calm in the moment, but afterward I let him say what he needed to say.

follow_ups.question: Did your family file a complaint?
follow_ups.response: No. We did not think it would go anywhere, and that is part of the problem.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested. I have a nephew who had a DUI years ago, and that shook the family, but he got through it.

follow_ups.question: Was anyone close to you incarcerated?
follow_ups.response: No one in my immediate family.

follow_ups.question: How did the family respond to your nephew's DUI?
follow_ups.response: There was disappointment, but also help. His mother made sure he got rides and did what the court required.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in presidential elections and most local elections, but I have missed some smaller ones. Washington makes voting by mail pretty easy, so Rosa and I sit at the table with the pamphlet. I like reading the local measures because those affect roads, schools, and taxes. I do not put signs in my yard or argue online. Voting is enough noise for me.

follow_ups.question: Who usually fills out the ballot first, you or Rosa?
follow_ups.response: Rosa usually starts first. I take longer because I read more of the pamphlet, especially taxes.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics with your children?
follow_ups.response: A little, but not at Sunday dinner if I can help it. My kids are more outspoken than me.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would call myself moderate, maybe independent, but I lean toward Democrats on health care, Social Security, and how working people are treated. I do not like waste, and I do not like politicians promising everything with no way to pay for it. But I also know what it is to work hard and still need help, so I do not look down on people using programs. Immigration is personal to me because my parents came from Mexico and worked hard their whole lives. I care about safe neighborhoods, fair policing, decent schools, and keeping Medicare and Social Security strong. I am not interested in shouting politics; I want practical people who remember regular families.

follow_ups.question: What issues most affect your vote?
follow_ups.response: Health care costs, Social Security, property taxes, immigration fairness, and whether local leaders take care of roads and seniors.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever strongly identified with one party?
follow_ups.response: Not strongly. I have voted more often Democratic, but I still read the person and the measure.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more protective of programs for older people because now I see how much they matter. When I was younger I thought mostly about work and taxes. Now I see friends choosing between prescriptions, groceries, and home repairs. I also pay more attention to how people talk about immigrants. Some talk like families like mine are a problem, and I do not accept that.

follow_ups.question: Did retirement change your political thinking?
follow_ups.response: Yes. A fixed income makes you notice every policy that touches medicine, utilities, and property tax.

follow_ups.question: What has not changed?
follow_ups.response: I still believe people should work if they can, take care of family, and not waste money.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: It affected me somewhat. I am not Black, so I do not pretend it is the same experience, but I know what it is like to be looked at as suspicious because of your skin or accent. Seeing the videos on television made me sad and angry. I also worried when protests turned tense, because then people stop listening to the main point. For me the main point is that police should be accountable and people should be treated with dignity.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk about it at home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly with Rosa and my sons. My grandchildren talked about it more directly than we did.

follow_ups.question: Did it change how you view local policing?
follow_ups.response: It made me pay more attention to who is running for sheriff or city council and what they say about training.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the issues are real, especially when families say the same things for years and nobody listens. My way of thinking is practical: if officers have power, there should be rules, cameras, training, and consequences when they abuse it. I also think communities need police when something dangerous happens, so I am not for pretending there is no need. But respect has to go both ways, and the person with the badge has more responsibility. That is how I see it.

follow_ups.question: Do your friends agree with you?
follow_ups.response: Some do, some think the protests went too far. We usually keep it calm at cards because nobody wants to ruin the afternoon.

follow_ups.question: Where do you get information about these issues?
follow_ups.response: Local news, public radio sometimes, the voter pamphlet, and what my kids send me, though I check before believing everything.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think the country talks about race in waves, then gets tired and tries to move on, but people living it do not get to move on. In my own life, being Mexican American meant people sometimes assumed I was less educated, which maybe I was on paper, but they also assumed less capable. My grandchildren are more comfortable naming things as racism than I was. I grew up swallowing a lot because that felt safer. Now I think speaking plainly is better, if you can do it without hating people.

follow_ups.question: Have your grandchildren changed how you talk about race?
follow_ups.response: Yes. They use words I did not use, like systemic racism. I listen, even when I would say it simpler.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about Mexican American identity with them?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly through food, Spanish sayings, music, and stories about my parents.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with family and a few friends, but I have not joined protests. At my age I am more likely to vote, listen, and speak up at the table.

follow_ups.question: What do you say when you speak up?
follow_ups.response: I say people should not dismiss someone's experience just because it did not happen to them.

follow_ups.question: Would you attend a local meeting about policing?
follow_ups.response: Maybe, especially if it was at the senior center or church and not too late at night.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My grandchildren are the most engaged. They posted things online and talked about marches, though I do not know if all of them went. My sons are practical like me but more direct. Rosa worries about conflict and prays for peace. Some friends at the senior center think the subject is uncomfortable, and they change it to baseball pretty fast.

follow_ups.question: Has it caused arguments in your family?
follow_ups.response: Small arguments, not breaks. Mostly the younger ones push us to say more clearly where we stand.

follow_ups.question: Who do you think influenced your views most?
follow_ups.response: My own parents' life and my grandchildren's questions. Those two together keep me honest.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: For 75, I am doing all right, but I have hypertension and some arthritis in my knees and hands. I take blood pressure medicine and try to check my numbers most mornings. My doctor wants me walking, eating less salt, and losing a few pounds. I have cataracts starting, not bad enough for surgery yet. I can still garden and do light repairs, but I pace myself now.

follow_ups.question: What medications do you take regularly?
follow_ups.response: A blood pressure pill every morning and sometimes acetaminophen for knee pain. I try not to take too much.

follow_ups.question: What health issue bothers you most day to day?
follow_ups.response: The knees, because they decide how long I can walk or kneel in the garden.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Walking club makes it easier because if people expect you, you go. Rosa also helps by cooking lighter with me. What makes it hard is habit: I like salty food, I like sitting with a game on, and rain makes walking less inviting. Money matters too, because fresh food and dental care are not cheap.

follow_ups.question: What healthy habit has stuck best?
follow_ups.response: The morning blood pressure check and walking twice a week.

follow_ups.question: What habit is hardest to change?
follow_ups.response: Salt. I grew up with strong flavors, and my hand still reaches before my brain stops it.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: The main thing was my blood pressure getting too high last year. The doctor adjusted my medication and told me to take it seriously. I also had a bad knee flare after overdoing it in the garden last spring, and I had to use a cane for about a week. Nothing broken, no hospital stay. It was enough to remind me I cannot work like I am 45.

follow_ups.question: What were you doing when your knee flared?
follow_ups.response: Digging and turning soil for tomatoes. I kept going too long because I wanted the rows straight.

follow_ups.question: Did you follow up with the doctor?
follow_ups.response: Yes, for the blood pressure. For the knee, I rested, iced it, and mentioned it at the next appointment.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: Health gets in the way mostly by slowing me down. I can still care for Rosa and the house, but I take breaks and do fewer ladder jobs.

follow_ups.question: What tasks have you stopped doing?
follow_ups.response: Roof work, tall ladders, and heavy brake jobs. Those are for younger backs.

follow_ups.question: Do you worry about caring for Rosa?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a little. I want to stay strong enough to help her without becoming another burden.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Rosa has diabetes, controlled but always there. She watches her sugar and has regular appointments. When her feet hurt or she is tired, I do more around the house. My sister Teresa also had a heart scare, and that made me think about how far apart we all are now. Family health is like weather: even when it is not storming at your house, you keep an eye on the sky.

follow_ups.question: How do you help Rosa manage diabetes?
follow_ups.response: I drive her to appointments, help cook less sugary meals, and remind her to check her feet when she has been walking.

follow_ups.question: Does her health affect your schedule?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes. If she has an appointment or a bad day, I skip the senior center without making a fuss.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: Medicare helps a lot, but the bills still make you pay attention. Appointments can take time, and specialists are not always close. I have put off dental work because it was expensive, and Rosa has delayed buying new glasses before. We do not skip blood pressure or diabetes medicine. Those are not optional. But yes, some care waits because the budget says wait.

follow_ups.question: What care have you delayed most recently?
follow_ups.response: Dental cleaning and a crown the dentist mentioned. I am saving before I decide.

follow_ups.question: How do you choose what cannot wait?
follow_ups.response: Medicine, diabetes checks, blood pressure, and anything with pain that does not go away. Teeth and glasses sometimes get pushed.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: We use home remedies, but not instead of the doctor for serious things. Manzanilla tea for stomach, Vicks on the chest when we were kids, warm compresses, caldo when someone is sick. My mother believed in certain teas and prayers, and some of that stays with you. I do not take mystery pills or things that interfere with medicine. I respect both the old ways and the doctor's office.

follow_ups.question: What remedy do you still use most?
follow_ups.response: Chamomile tea and hot broth. It is comfort as much as medicine.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever used a curandero?
follow_ups.response: No, not personally. My mother knew people who did, but our family mostly used home remedies and church prayers.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I quit cigarettes many years ago after my children complained about the smell and my doctor warned me. I drink a beer once in a while with a game or at a family barbecue, but not every day. When I am stressed, I am more likely to go outside, pull weeds, or make something with my hands. That calms me better than drinking.

follow_ups.question: When did you quit smoking?
follow_ups.response: In my forties. It was not easy, but Rosa kept the pressure on me.

follow_ups.question: How many drinks would you have in a typical week?
follow_ups.response: Most weeks none, sometimes one or two beers if there is family over or a Seahawks game.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I take what is prescribed for blood pressure, and I use over-the-counter pain medicine for my knees when I need it. I do not use marijuana. I know people my age who use gummies for sleep or pain, but I am cautious because I do not like feeling out of control. The most recent pain medicine was last week after kneeling too long near the tomato plants. I took acetaminophen with dinner and went to bed early.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever been offered stronger pain medication?
follow_ups.response: After a dental procedure years ago, yes, but I only took a little. I did not like the foggy feeling.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever use sleep medication?
follow_ups.response: No. If I cannot sleep, I read a few pages or say prayers.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: We use Medicare, supplemental coverage, and careful budgeting. Every month I set aside money for prescriptions, copays, and the things insurance does not cover. Rosa and I compare pharmacy prices when something changes. Our children would help if it got serious, but I do not want to ask unless we really need it. Pride and budget live close together in my house.

follow_ups.question: About how much do medical costs run monthly?
follow_ups.response: It changes, but between premiums, prescriptions, and copays, a few hundred dollars is normal.

follow_ups.question: Do you use one pharmacy?
follow_ups.response: Mostly the same pharmacy because they know us, but I check prices if a medication jumps.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I believe in vaccines. I got the COVID shots, flu shots, and what my doctor recommends for older people.

follow_ups.question: Were you hesitant at first?
follow_ups.response: A little with the first COVID shot because everything felt fast, but I talked to my doctor and decided it was safer.

follow_ups.question: Does Rosa feel the same?
follow_ups.response: Yes. With diabetes, she takes that seriously.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: My doctor is number one. I also listen to the pharmacist and read what comes from the county health department. My daughter Elena works around medical offices, so I ask her when I do not understand something. I do not trust random Facebook posts, especially when they sound too angry or too certain. For health, I want someone who has to answer for what they tell me.

follow_ups.question: Do you read information in Spanish or English?
follow_ups.response: Mostly English now, but if something is complicated I like having Spanish too.

follow_ups.question: Have you corrected misinformation in your family?
follow_ups.response: A couple times. I usually say, ask your doctor, not your cousin's internet page.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: This past year I have felt mostly steady, but with more worry than I like to admit. Money, health, and Rosa's diabetes sit in the back of my mind. I enjoy the garden and the senior center, and those keep me from sitting too much with my thoughts. Some days I feel proud that we made a good life. Other days I miss people who are gone, especially my parents and old work friends. I am not miserable, but I know I am older now.

follow_ups.question: When do worries usually show up?
follow_ups.response: At night, after the house is quiet. That is when I start adding bills in my head.

follow_ups.question: What helps you feel steady again?
follow_ups.response: Morning routine, prayer, working in the garden, and having coffee with someone who knows me.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: Last winter I had a rough week after a friend from the senior center died. His name was Bill, and he used to sit near the window and complain about the coffee. After the funeral I came home and felt the house was too quiet. I went out to the shed and could not find my garden shears, and for some reason that made me angry enough to slam a drawer. Rosa came out and just stood with me. It was not about the shears. It was about losing another person from my age group.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk to anyone about that grief?
follow_ups.response: Mostly Rosa and Frank. I did not call it grief right away, but that is what it was.

follow_ups.question: Did it change your routine?
follow_ups.response: For a week I skipped walking club. Then Frank called and said, come on, and I went.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have worry, maybe anxiety, but I have never been diagnosed with anything. My doctor once suggested talking to someone, but I did not go. Part of me doubts therapy would help a man like me, and part of me knows that may be stubbornness. I do get down sometimes, especially in dark months. I cope by staying busy, praying, walking, and keeping my hands useful.

follow_ups.question: What makes you doubt therapy?
follow_ups.response: I was raised to handle things privately. Paying someone to talk still feels strange to me.

follow_ups.question: Would you consider it if things got worse?
follow_ups.response: Maybe. If Rosa or my doctor pushed hard enough, I would listen.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: Everyone has stress. My children worry about work, bills, and their own kids, and Rosa worries about all of us.

follow_ups.question: Who in the family seems most stressed?
follow_ups.response: Elena, because medical office work wears her out and she still helps her children.

follow_ups.question: How does the family support each other?
follow_ups.response: Phone calls, food, rides, and showing up when someone has an appointment or a repair problem.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I was raised Catholic, and I still identify as Catholic. Rosa and I go to Mass most Sundays, though not every single week if health or weather gets in the way. Religion for me is family, memory, prayer, and trying to be decent. I like Christmas Posadas, Dia de los Muertos, lighting a candle, and hearing old hymns in Spanish. I am not someone who quotes scripture at people, but faith gives shape to my week. When I worry at night, I pray before I start counting bills again.

follow_ups.question: Are you involved in church activities?
follow_ups.response: Rosa is more involved. I help with setup sometimes, carry tables, fix a cabinet, or bring food.

follow_ups.question: What religious holidays matter most to you?
follow_ups.response: Christmas, Posadas, Easter, and Dia de los Muertos for remembering family.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.
transcript.response: I use Facebook a little, mostly to see family pictures, church announcements, and community posts. I do not post much. Sometimes I watch repair videos on YouTube if I want to see how someone else handles a part or a tool. My grandchildren send pictures by text more than social media. I am careful because there is too much arguing and too many fake stories online. I would rather talk in person.

follow_ups.question: How often do you check Facebook?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once a day, sometimes less. Usually in the evening after dinner.

follow_ups.question: What do you watch on YouTube?
follow_ups.response: Tool repair, gardening tips, old mariachi performances, and sometimes Mariners highlights.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they use Facebook or Twitter to get (emotional or financial) support during tough times. What about you?
transcript.response: No, I do not ask for support online. If I need help, I call family or talk to someone at church.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever donated to someone online?
follow_ups.response: Once or twice for local families, but small amounts. I like to know it is real.

follow_ups.question: Where do you turn first in a tough time?
follow_ups.response: Rosa first, then my children, then church friends if it is something practical.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your level of stress, worry, and your emotional coping strategies.
transcript.response: Stress has gone up with prices and health appointments. I cope more deliberately now by walking, checking the budget, praying, and not watching too much news.

follow_ups.question: What news do you limit?
follow_ups.response: Cable arguments and repeated crime stories. They raise my blood pressure without solving anything.

follow_ups.question: What coping strategy works fastest?
follow_ups.response: Going outside with a small task, like watering or sharpening a tool.

transcript.question_text: This might be repetitive, but before we go on to the next section, I want to quickly make sure I have this right: who are you living with right now?
transcript.response: I live with my wife, Rosa. It is just the two of us in our Puyallup home.

follow_ups.question: No adult children living there?
follow_ups.response: No, they all have their own homes.

follow_ups.question: No other relatives living there?
follow_ups.response: No, only visits.

transcript.question_text: Any babies or small children?
transcript.response: No babies or small children live with us.

follow_ups.question: Do small children visit?
follow_ups.response: Younger grandchildren visit, but they do not live here.

follow_ups.question: How often are children in the house?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a couple Sundays a month.

transcript.question_text: Anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody like that.

follow_ups.question: No one away temporarily?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Has that been stable all year?
follow_ups.response: Yes.

transcript.question_text: Any lodgers, boarders, or employees who live here?
transcript.response: No lodgers, boarders, or employees.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever rented a room?
follow_ups.response: No, Rosa would not like that.

follow_ups.question: Do you host anyone for long visits?
follow_ups.response: Not long visits, only family for a night or two.

transcript.question_text: Who shares the responsibility for the rent, mortgage, or other household expenses?
transcript.response: Rosa and I share expenses from our retirement income.

follow_ups.question: Do children contribute monthly?
follow_ups.response: No, not regularly.

follow_ups.question: Who tracks the bills?
follow_ups.response: Mostly me, with Rosa checking.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to talk about how you make ends meet and what the monthly budget looks like for you and your family. What were your biggest expenses last month?
transcript.response: The biggest expenses were property tax savings, utilities, groceries, insurance, and medical costs. We also had a car repair last month, a battery and some brake work, so that made it higher.

follow_ups.question: Which bill surprised you most?
follow_ups.response: The car repair. I can do small things, but brakes are harder for me now.

follow_ups.question: How do you track those expenses?
follow_ups.response: Notebook, receipts in an envelope, and the bank statement.

transcript.question_text: How much did your household spend in the past month? Is that the usual amount? And if not, how much do you usually spend and on what?
transcript.response: Last month was around $3,400 because of the car. A more usual month is closer to $2,800 to $3,000 for utilities, groceries, insurance, gas, medicine, church giving, and household supplies.

follow_ups.question: What is the most flexible part of the budget?
follow_ups.response: Eating out, small gifts, and garden supplies. Those get cut first.

follow_ups.question: What is least flexible?
follow_ups.response: Medicine, utilities, insurance, and taxes.

transcript.question_text: Does your household own or rent your home?
transcript.response: We own our home. The mortgage is paid off, thank God, but taxes, insurance, and repairs still feel like a payment sometimes.

follow_ups.question: When did you pay off the mortgage?
follow_ups.response: About eight years ago. That was one of the proudest days for us.

follow_ups.question: Do you plan to stay there?
follow_ups.response: Yes, as long as stairs, health, and money allow.

transcript.question_text: Bills can fluctuate over the course of a year. Seasons change, there are holidays and special events, school starts and ends, and so on. Tell me all about how your bills have fluctuated over the past year.
transcript.response: Winter heating raises utilities, and summer water goes up if I am keeping the garden alive. Holidays mean food and gifts, especially Christmas and birthdays. Property taxes and insurance are the big ones I plan around. Medical costs come in waves depending on appointments.

follow_ups.question: Which season is hardest financially?
follow_ups.response: Winter, because heat and holidays come together.

follow_ups.question: How do you prepare for property taxes?
follow_ups.response: I set aside money monthly in a separate savings account.

transcript.question_text: Tell me all about how you coped with any extra expenses in the past months.
transcript.response: We used savings for the car repair and cut back on eating out and little store trips. I also postponed buying new garden tools.

follow_ups.question: Was there anything you repaired instead of replacing?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I fixed an old hose reel and sharpened old pruners instead of buying new ones.

follow_ups.question: Did you ask family for help?
follow_ups.response: No, not for that. We could handle it.

transcript.question_text: Some people have a savings account, some people save in a different way, and some people say they don't save. How about you?
transcript.response: We have a small savings account. It is not big, but it is important to me. I also keep some cash at home for emergencies, the old habit from my parents. Saving on a fixed income means slow and steady, not big amounts. If there is money left at the end of the month, I move a little before it disappears.

follow_ups.question: What amount makes you feel comfortable?
follow_ups.response: Enough to cover a car repair or a medical bill without panic, maybe a few thousand if possible.

follow_ups.question: Do you save automatically?
follow_ups.response: Not automatically through a computer. I move it myself after the checks come in.

transcript.question_text: Some people save for big things, like a home, while others save for a rainy day. How about for you (in the last year)?
transcript.response: Mostly rainy day. At this stage I am not saving for a bigger house or anything like that. I save for medical surprises, car repairs, property taxes, and maybe a short trip with Rosa. I would like to go back to Victoria or the San Juan Islands if we can do it without worrying the whole time. I also want a little money for grandchildren's graduations.

follow_ups.question: What trip are you most likely to take?
follow_ups.response: A short road trip to the San Juan Islands, maybe two nights, packed food, simple motel.

follow_ups.question: Do you save for visiting family in Mexico?
follow_ups.response: I dream about Jalisco, but the cost and my health make it stay in the planning stage.

transcript.question_text: Some people have student loans or credit card debt. Others take out loans from family or friends or find other ways of borrowing money. Tell me about all the debts you're paying on right now.
transcript.response: No student loans. We use a credit card but pay it off most months. The mortgage is gone, and we do not owe family money.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever carry a credit card balance?
follow_ups.response: Only once in a while after a big repair, and I try to pay it down fast.

follow_ups.question: Are you comfortable borrowing from family?
follow_ups.response: Not really. I would rather cut back first.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any time during the past year that you haven't had enough money to buy something that you needed or pay a bill that was due.
transcript.response: We have not missed a bill, but we have delayed things. Dental work for me waited, and Rosa put off glasses for a couple months. There were weeks when groceries were more careful, more beans, rice, soup, and less meat. I know that is still better than many people have it. But the feeling of counting every dollar is familiar.

follow_ups.question: What do you buy when groceries need to stretch?
follow_ups.response: Beans, rice, eggs, tortillas, chicken thighs if on sale, hominy, and vegetables from the garden.

follow_ups.question: What bill worries you most?
follow_ups.response: Medical and dental because you do not always know the amount until afterward.

transcript.question_text: What is or was your occupation? In this occupation, what kind of work do you do and what are the most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: I was a handyman and repairman for most of my working life. I fixed leaky faucets, patched walls, repaired doors, built shelves, replaced trim, painted rooms, repaired fences, and did small carpentry jobs. The most important duties were showing up, figuring out the problem, doing the work cleanly, and charging fairly. I worked for homeowners, landlords, and sometimes small businesses. I did not have fancy schooling, so my reputation was my certificate. If people trusted me in their house, I had to honor that.

follow_ups.question: What kind of job did you enjoy most?
follow_ups.response: Small carpentry where the result looked neat, like a door that finally closed right or shelves that fit perfectly.

follow_ups.question: What job did you dislike?
follow_ups.response: Emergency plumbing under a sink in a cramped cabinet. My shoulders still remember those.

transcript.question_text: Was your occupation covered by a union or employee association contract?
transcript.response: No, not most of my handyman work. I had some construction jobs around union people, but I was mostly independent or informal.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever want union work?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, for the benefits. But by then I was already making my own way.

follow_ups.question: How did no union affect retirement?
follow_ups.response: It meant no pension from that work, just Social Security and what we saved.

transcript.question_text: In the past year, how many weeks did you work (for a few hours, including paid vacation, paid sick leave, and military service)?
transcript.response: For pay, zero weeks. Volunteer work, many weeks, but I do not count that as employment.

follow_ups.question: How many weeks did you volunteer?
follow_ups.response: Probably forty weeks or so, depending on appointments and weather.

follow_ups.question: Did you receive any paid vacation or sick leave?
follow_ups.response: No, I am retired.

transcript.question_text: How many hours each week did you usually work?
transcript.response: For pay, none now. Volunteering is usually three to six hours a week.

follow_ups.question: Was that different before retirement?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I often worked forty hours or more when jobs were steady.

follow_ups.question: Do volunteer hours vary?
follow_ups.response: Yes, spring garden season is busier.

transcript.question_text: In the past week, did you work for pay (even for 1 hour) at a job or business?
transcript.response: No, I did not work for pay last week.

follow_ups.question: Did you do any unpaid work last week?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I helped at the senior center and fixed a neighbor's loose latch.

follow_ups.question: Did you receive any cash for that?
follow_ups.response: No, just a thank you and coffee.

transcript.question_text: Did you have more than one job or business, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: No. I have no paid job or business now.

follow_ups.question: Any side business still active?
follow_ups.response: No, I closed that chapter.

follow_ups.question: Do people still ask you to work?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but I usually say I can recommend someone or help only lightly.

transcript.question_text: Now, in the past month, how many jobs did you work, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: Zero paid jobs in the past month.

follow_ups.question: Any paid handyman calls?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Any unpaid workshops?
follow_ups.response: Yes, two senior center workshops.

transcript.question_text: For your job or occupations, how much money did you receive in the past month?
transcript.response: From jobs, nothing. My income is retirement income, mainly Social Security, not wages.

follow_ups.question: Do you receive any volunteer stipend?
follow_ups.response: No stipend.

follow_ups.question: Do people give gifts for help?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes food, but not money I count as income.

transcript.question_text: How often do you get paid?
transcript.response: Social Security comes monthly.

follow_ups.question: Is it predictable?
follow_ups.response: Yes, very predictable, and I plan around that.

follow_ups.question: Does Rosa also receive monthly income?
follow_ups.response: Yes, her Social Security is monthly too.

transcript.question_text: In total, how much did your household make in the past month?
transcript.response: Together, Rosa and I brought in about $3,300 last month from Social Security and a very small retirement account withdrawal. Some months are closer to $3,100 if we do not draw extra.

follow_ups.question: Is that before or after deductions?
follow_ups.response: That is roughly what we have to work with after the usual deductions.

follow_ups.question: Do you expect that income to change?
follow_ups.response: Only with cost-of-living adjustments or if we need to draw more savings.

transcript.question_text: Switching gears a bit, let's talk a little about tax time. Did you file taxes last year (the most recent year)?
transcript.response: Yes, we filed taxes last year. My son Luis helped us use a simple tax program and check the forms.

follow_ups.question: Do you usually owe or get a refund?
follow_ups.response: Usually small either way. Nothing dramatic.

follow_ups.question: Do you keep paper records?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I keep a folder with statements and receipts.

transcript.question_text: Tell me more about your workplace. How long have you been at your current job? How would you describe the benefits that come with your job? (This could include things like health benefits, paid time off, vacation, and sick time.)
transcript.response: I do not have a current job, so there are no workplace benefits. My health coverage is through Medicare.

follow_ups.question: Did your old handyman work have benefits?
follow_ups.response: No, that was one of the hard parts.

follow_ups.question: Does volunteering provide anything formal?
follow_ups.response: No, just community and coffee.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your relationships at work? (How is your relationship with your manager or boss? How are your relationships with your coworkers?)
transcript.response: No job now, but at the senior center I get along well with staff and other volunteers.

follow_ups.question: Who coordinates your workshops?
follow_ups.response: A staff member named Linda usually puts me on the calendar.

follow_ups.question: Any conflicts there?
follow_ups.response: Only small teasing with Frank about whose repair method is better.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about how predictable your work schedule is. How would you describe your job in terms of flexibility with your hours?
transcript.response: Since I am retired, my schedule is flexible. Volunteer sessions are scheduled, but if I have a doctor appointment or Rosa needs me, I can change it. That is one of the gifts of retirement. When I was working, the schedule depended on customers and emergencies, so it could be unpredictable. Now I prefer a routine, but I do not like being rushed.

follow_ups.question: How far ahead are workshops planned?
follow_ups.response: Usually two or three weeks, sometimes a month.

follow_ups.question: Do you prefer mornings or afternoons?
follow_ups.response: Late morning. Too early and people are not awake, too late and I lose energy.

transcript.question_text: Some people say it's hard to take or keep a job because of child care. How about for you?
transcript.response: Not for me now. My children are adults.

follow_ups.question: Was child care hard when they were young?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but Rosa handled most of that, and family helped.

follow_ups.question: Do you provide child care now?
follow_ups.response: Only occasional grandparent help.

transcript.question_text: Do you receive any payments or benefits from SNAP, food stamps, housing voucher payments, supplemental security income, or any other programs like that?
transcript.response: No SNAP or housing voucher. We receive Social Security and Medicare.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever applied for food assistance?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Would you if things got tight?
follow_ups.response: If we truly needed it, yes, though I would try other ways first.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about times over the last year when your income was especially low. And tell me about all the things you did to make ends meet during that time.
transcript.response: The income is steady, so it is not low one month and high the next. The problem is when expenses jump. We made ends meet by using savings, cooking at home, postponing purchases, and doing repairs myself when safe.

follow_ups.question: What purchase did you postpone?
follow_ups.response: Garden shears and new shoes for walking. I made the old ones last longer.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever sell things?
follow_ups.response: Not often. I would rather fix and keep what we have.

transcript.question_text: What would it be like for you if you had to spend $400 for an emergency? Would you have the money, and if not, how would you get it?
transcript.response: We could cover $400, but I would feel it. It would probably come from savings, and then I would tighten the next month to build it back.

follow_ups.question: Would you use a credit card?
follow_ups.response: Maybe first for the points or timing, but I would pay it from savings.

follow_ups.question: What emergency is most likely?
follow_ups.response: Car, plumbing, or medical copay.

transcript.question_text: Overall, how do you feel about your financial situation?
transcript.response: I feel stable but cautious. We are not poor the way my parents were at times, and owning the house gives us security. But fixed income means every increase in groceries, insurance, or taxes takes a bite. I am proud we paid our bills and raised our children. I also know one major health problem could change the picture fast. So I am grateful, but I keep my pencil sharp.

follow_ups.question: What would make you feel more secure?
follow_ups.response: Lower medical and dental costs, and knowing property taxes would not jump too much.

follow_ups.question: Do you consider yourself financially disciplined?
follow_ups.response: Yes, though I still splurge on tools or good ingredients once in a while.

transcript.question_text: Are you now married, widowed, divorced, separated, or have you never been married? If you are not currently married, are you currently living with a romantic partner?
transcript.response: I am married to Rosa, and we live together.

follow_ups.question: How long have you been married?
follow_ups.response: A little over fifty years.

follow_ups.question: Is this your first marriage?
follow_ups.response: Yes.

transcript.question_text: For our records, we also need your date of birth. Could you please provide that?

follow_ups.question: So you are 75 now?
follow_ups.response: Yes, 75.

follow_ups.question: Do you usually celebrate your birthday?
follow_ups.response: Small family dinner, nothing big.

transcript.question_text: Were you born in the United States? If you were not born in the U.S., what country were you born, and what year did you first come to the U.S. to live?
transcript.response: Yes, I was born in the United States. My parents were born in Mexico.

follow_ups.question: Where in Mexico were your parents from?
follow_ups.response: Jalisco.

follow_ups.question: Did Spanish or English come first for you?
follow_ups.response: Spanish at home came first, then English at school.

transcript.question_text: What city and state were you born in?
transcript.response: Yakima, Washington.

follow_ups.question: Did you grow up there?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly around Yakima until my twenties.

follow_ups.question: Do you still visit?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes to see my sister Teresa.

transcript.question_text: Are you of Hispanic, Latinx, or Spanish origin?
transcript.response: Yes, Mexican American.

follow_ups.question: Do you use Hispanic, Latino, or Mexican American most?
follow_ups.response: Mexican American.

follow_ups.question: Is that identity important to you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, very.

transcript.question_text: What race or races do you identify with?
transcript.response: I usually mark White and Hispanic or Mexican American, depending on the form. Sometimes the race question does not fit very well.

follow_ups.question: Do you identify as Indigenous?
follow_ups.response: Not formally. My family talked about mixed roots, but I do not claim a tribe.

follow_ups.question: How do you answer when forms are limited?
follow_ups.response: I choose Hispanic or Mexican if available, and White if race is separate.

transcript.question_text: What is the highest degree or grade you've completed?
transcript.response: Tenth grade. I did not receive a high school diploma.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever get a GED?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.response: Only informal workshops and learning from other workers.

transcript.question_text: Are you enrolled in school?
transcript.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Any classes at the senior center?
follow_ups.response: Only workshops, not school enrollment.

follow_ups.question: Would you take a class now?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a short one, not for grades.

transcript.question_text: Have you been enrolled in school during the past 3 months?
transcript.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Any online courses?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Any formal training?
follow_ups.response: No formal training.

transcript.question_text: Have you ever served on active duty in the U.S. Armed Forces, Reserves, or National Guard?
transcript.response: No, I never served.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone in your family serve?
follow_ups.response: A cousin did, but not me.

follow_ups.question: Were you ever close to joining?
follow_ups.response: No, I went straight into work.

transcript.question_text: What religion do you identify with, if any?
transcript.response: Roman Catholic.

follow_ups.question: Practicing Catholic?
follow_ups.response: Yes, though not perfect attendance.

follow_ups.question: Is Rosa Catholic too?
follow_ups.response: Yes.

transcript.question_text: Generally speaking, do you usually think of yourself as a Democrat, a Republican, an Independent, or what? And how strongly do you associate with that party?
transcript.response: I think of myself as an Independent who leans Democratic. I am not a strong party person. I vote for Democrats more often because of health care, Social Security, immigration, and working families. But I still look at the candidate and the local issue. follow_ups.question: Was that the same household you grew up in?

follow_ups.question: What was the neighborhood like?

follow_ups.question: Were they still married then?

follow_ups.question: Who set the rules at home?

transcript.question_text: Who else did you live with?

follow_ups.question: Were you the oldest?

follow_ups.question: Was the house crowded?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but that was normal to us.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your dad completed?
transcript.response: Maybe sixth grade in Mexico.

follow_ups.question: Could he read and write?
follow_ups.response: Yes, in Spanish, but not comfortably in English.

follow_ups.question: Did he value school?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but work came first in his life.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your mom completed?
transcript.response: Around fourth or fifth grade.

follow_ups.question: Was that in Mexico?
follow_ups.response: Yes, in Jalisco.

follow_ups.question: Did she read at home?
follow_ups.response: Prayer cards, letters, recipes, things like that.

transcript.question_text: Did your mom work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, she did.

follow_ups.question: Was it full time?
follow_ups.response: Seasonal and sometimes part time, depending on harvest and family needs.

follow_ups.question: Did she also run the household?
follow_ups.response: Yes, she worked and still kept the home together.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My mother worked in fruit packing and sometimes cleaning. In the packing house she sorted, packed, and handled apples and other fruit. Her important duties were moving fast, keeping quality right, and standing for long hours. At home she cooked, sewed, managed money, and raised us.

follow_ups.question: Did she like that work?
follow_ups.response: She did not complain much, but it was hard on her body.

follow_ups.question: What did you learn from her work?
follow_ups.response: Endurance and not wasting food or money.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: It was agricultural packing work around Yakima. The business handled fruit from growers, mostly apples when I remember it. They sorted, boxed, and shipped produce. Cleaning jobs were in offices or homes, whatever she could get.

follow_ups.question: Was the workforce mostly immigrant families?
follow_ups.response: Many Mexican families, yes, and other working people from the area.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever visit her workplace?
follow_ups.response: A few times outside, waiting for her. I remember the smell of fruit and cardboard.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, always.

follow_ups.question: Was his work steady?
follow_ups.response: Seasonal at first, then steadier when he got maintenance work.

follow_ups.question: Did he ever stop working?
follow_ups.response: Only when his body forced him later in life.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My father did farm labor, orchard work, and later maintenance. He pruned, picked, lifted, repaired equipment, and fixed things around worker housing. His most important duty was doing whatever needed doing without making a speech about it. I learned tools by watching him.

follow_ups.question: Was he skilled with repairs?
follow_ups.response: Very skilled, though nobody gave him a certificate for it.

follow_ups.question: What tool reminds you of him?
follow_ups.response: A worn hammer with tape on the handle. He could make it do anything.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: He worked for farms, orchards, and later a property maintenance outfit connected to agricultural housing. The farms grew fruit and other crops. The maintenance work kept buildings, fences, pumps, and equipment usable. It was practical work, the kind people only notice when it is not done.

follow_ups.question: Did his work influence your career?
follow_ups.response: Completely. I became the man people called to fix things because that is what I saw him do.

follow_ups.question: Did he want something different for you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, he wanted me to have steadier work and less strain, even if he did not say it softly.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope Rosa and I are still in our house, still able to cook, go to church, and sit in the garden. I hope my blood pressure stays controlled and her diabetes does not get worse. I want to keep volunteering at the senior center, maybe not lifting much, but teaching what I know. I also want to finish a handwritten family cookbook with tamales, pozole rojo, salsa verde, and the little tricks my mother used. I hope the grandchildren remember where they come from, not in a heavy way, but through food, language, music, and stories. Mostly I hope to stay useful without pretending I am young.

follow_ups.question: What recipe would go first in the cookbook?
follow_ups.response: My mother's pork tamales, with notes about soaking the husks and not rushing the masa.

follow_ups.question: What would you like your grandchildren to learn from you?
follow_ups.response: How to fix simple things, how to stretch money, and how to respect family history.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: Family, health, faith, and being useful. I value keeping my word and doing a job correctly, even a small one. I value the old ways from my parents, but also the quiet life Rosa and I made here in Puyallup. Money matters because it protects peace, but it is not the point by itself. The point is to have enough, share when you can, and leave something good behind.

follow_ups.question: What does being useful mean now?
follow_ups.response: Helping Rosa, teaching at the senior center, feeding family, and fixing what I still can.

follow_ups.question: What do you want people to remember about you?
follow_ups.response: That I showed up, worked honestly, and kept the family close.
